lessonTitle: Principles of Oncology: Treatment Modalities, Emergencies and Performance Status

blocks.text: A 58-year-old woman is ten days into her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer. She feels shivery and a little unwell, her thermometer reads 38.3 C, and she says she will wait until her routine appointment on Thursday rather than bother anyone. Within hours this could become a life-threatening infection, and the single most useful thing you can teach her is when not to wait.

blocks.markdown: Cancer treatment is built on three questions. **What is the extent of disease?** (staging, commonly by the TNM system: tumour size or invasion, nodal involvement, distant metastasis). **What is the goal of treatment?** **Is this patient fit enough for it?** The first guides the options, the second sets how much toxicity is acceptable, and the third decides whether the benefit will outweigh the harm.

blocks.title: Goals of treatment
blocks.text: **Curative**: aims to eradicate the cancer. **Adjuvant** therapy is given after definitive local treatment (usually surgery) to reduce the risk of recurrence by treating microscopic residual disease. **Neoadjuvant** therapy is given before surgery or radiotherapy to shrink the tumour or treat micrometastases. **Palliative** therapy aims to control symptoms, maintain quality of life and, where possible, prolong survival without cure.

rows: Surgery
Physical removal of tumour with margins and nodes
Curative for localised solid tumours; also debulking and palliation; operative risk
Radiotherapy
Ionising radiation damages DNA of dividing cells in a defined field
Local control, curative or palliative (for example bone pain); skin, mucosal and organ-specific damage in the field
Cytotoxic chemotherapy
Drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells
Adjuvant, neoadjuvant, palliative, curative in some haematological cancers and germ cell tumours; myelosuppression, nausea, alopecia, mucositis
Endocrine therapy
Blocks hormone signalling (for example oestrogen in breast cancer, androgens in prostate cancer)
Hormone receptor-positive tumours; hot flushes, bone loss, other drug-specific effects
Targeted therapy
Inhibits specific molecular drivers (for example HER2 or kinase mutations)
Tumours with a matching biomarker; drug-specific toxicity
Immunotherapy
Releases immune checkpoint inhibition so T cells attack tumour
Selected cancers; immune-related adverse effects (colitis, pneumonitis, endocrine disorders)
blocks.caption: Main modalities of cancer treatment. Regimens and doses are protocol-driven and specialist-prescribed.
Mosteller formula for body surface area, the unit by which many cytotoxic drugs are dosed (mg per m2). Dosing is protocol-specific and done by oncology pharmacy.

blocks.markdown: **Neutropenic sepsis.** Most cytotoxic drugs suppress the bone marrow, causing a nadir in the neutrophil count usually 7 to 14 days after treatment. **Neutropenia** is defined as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 1.0 x 10^9/L or below in many guidelines, and NICE defines a neutrophil count of 0.5 x 10^9/L or below (or expected to fall to that) with a temperature above 38 C or other signs of sepsis as neutropenic sepsis. Because neutrophils produce the usual signs of local inflammation, infection may present with only fever or malaise and rapidly progress to septic shock. Neutropenic sepsis is a **medical emergency**: take cultures and give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (NICE recommends empirical piperacillin with tazobactam unless contraindicated) within 1 hour of presentation, without waiting for the neutrophil count result, and manage as sepsis. Check doses and local protocol.

blocks.caption: ANC = absolute neutrophil count in 10^9/L. WBC = total white cell count in 10^9/L.

blocks.title: Calculating the absolute neutrophil count
blocks.prompt: On day 10 after chemotherapy, a patient has a temperature of 38.6 C and a full blood count showing a white cell count of 2.4 x 10^9/L with 15 percent neutrophils. Calculate the ANC and decide what to do.

steps.text: The ANC of 0.36 x 10^9/L is below 0.5 x 10^9/L, so she is neutropenic with fever, which meets the definition of neutropenic sepsis.

Treat as an emergency: blood cultures and lactate, then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (such as piperacillin with tazobactam per NICE, unless allergic or local policy differs) within 1 hour, IV fluids, monitoring and discussion with oncology. Do not wait for culture results or a review appointment.

blocks.answer: ANC is 0.36 x 10^9/L: neutropenic sepsis, requiring immediate IV antibiotics.

blocks.markdown: **Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC)** occurs when tumour in the vertebral column or epidural space compresses the cord or cauda equina. It is most often caused by breast, prostate, lung cancers and myeloma. Back pain is the earliest symptom, typically in the thoracic spine, worse lying flat or at night and with coughing or straining, sometimes band-like, followed by limb weakness, sensory loss, and bladder or bowel dysfunction. Once paralysis develops it is rarely reversible, so any patient with cancer and new back pain with neurological symptoms needs **urgent MRI of the whole spine** (NICE advises within 24 hours if neurological symptoms or signs are present, check current NG234). Management includes corticosteroids (for example dexamethasone per local protocol), analgesia, spinal precautions, and urgent oncology or spinal team input for radiotherapy or surgery. Other oncological emergencies include hypercalcaemia of malignancy, superior vena cava obstruction and tumour lysis syndrome.

**Performance status** is a standardised measure of a patient's functional ability that predicts tolerance of treatment and survival. The most widely used is the **ECOG scale (0 to 5)**; the Karnofsky scale is an alternative. Performance status is a clinical judgement of what the patient can do day to day (not age, and not the cancer alone) and it can change, so it is reassessed at each cycle.

rows: Fully active, no restriction
Restricted in strenuous activity but ambulatory and able to do light work
Ambulatory and capable of self-care but unable to work; up and about more than 50 percent of waking hours
Capable of only limited self-care; confined to bed or chair more than 50 percent of waking hours
Completely disabled; no self-care; totally confined to bed or chair
Dead
blocks.caption: ECOG performance status.

blocks.title: Using performance status
blocks.prompt: A 71-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer sleeps most of the day, needs help washing and dressing, and spends about 18 hours a day in bed or a chair. Would you offer standard cytotoxic chemotherapy?

steps.text: Assess function: he can only do limited self-care and is confined to bed or chair for well over 50 percent of waking hours, which is ECOG 3.

Evidence shows patients with ECOG 3 or 4 generally have poor tolerance of cytotoxic chemotherapy and often derive little benefit, while toxicity rises, so treatment is usually not offered, except in uncommon situations such as highly chemosensitive tumours where poor status is due to the cancer itself.
Discuss goals, preferences and best supportive care with the patient, involve palliative care early, and reassess if his function improves (for example with symptom control).
Document the performance status and the reasoning, because it is the key input to the multidisciplinary team discussion.

blocks.answer: ECOG 3: standard chemotherapy is generally not appropriate; focus on symptom control and supportive care and reassess if function changes.

items: Fever 38 C or above (or unwell) within weeks of chemotherapy: treat as neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; patients carry an alert card and a 24-hour contact number.
Cancer plus new back pain with neurological features: MSCC; urgent MRI whole spine.
Performance status guides fitness for chemotherapy: ECOG 0 to 1 are usually fit for standard treatment and trials; 2 needs careful discussion; 3 to 4 usually receive supportive care.
Adjuvant and neoadjuvant therapy are tied to surgery; palliative therapy aims to relieve symptoms and prolong useful life.

blocks.title: Do not wait for the blood count
blocks.text: Never delay antibiotics in a febrile patient on chemotherapy to wait for the neutrophil count. Treat first, as the consequences of delay can be septic shock and death.

points: Cancer treatment modalities (surgery, radiotherapy, cytotoxic chemotherapy, endocrine, targeted and immunotherapy) are chosen according to stage and tumour biology, with curative, adjuvant, neoadjuvant or palliative goals.

Neutropenic sepsis (ANC 0.5 x 10^9/L or below with fever) and metastatic spinal cord compression (cancer plus back pain with neurology) are emergencies requiring IV antibiotics within 1 hour and urgent whole-spine MRI respectively.
ECOG performance status (0 to 5) predicts tolerance of treatment; ECOG 3 to 4 patients generally do not benefit from standard cytotoxic chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with lymphoma has rigors when his central venous catheter is flushed on day 8 after chemotherapy. Temperature is 38.1 C, heart rate 110 and blood pressure 100/62; he looks unwell. His full blood count is pending. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wait for the blood count and give antibiotics only if neutropenic
Take cultures and give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour as for neutropenic sepsis, with fluids and monitoring
Give oral paracetamol and review in the morning
Arrange an outpatient review in 48 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Take cultures and give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour as for neutropenic sepsis, with fluids and monitoring

distractorRationale.a: Delay risks death from septic shock; treat first and check the count in parallel.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: febrile patients on chemotherapy are treated as neutropenic sepsis immediately.
distractorRationale.c: Paracetamol masks fever and delays treatment.

questions.explanation: Fever after chemotherapy should be assumed to be neutropenic sepsis until the blood count proves otherwise. Antibiotics are given within an hour without waiting for results.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer develops 2 weeks of thoracic back pain that is worse lying flat and at night, and now has leg heaviness and difficulty starting urination. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent MRI of the whole spine with steroids and oncology or spinal team involvement
Reassure that this is muscular back pain
Start oral NSAIDs and review in a month

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent MRI of the whole spine with steroids and oncology or spinal team involvement

distractorRationale.a: Radiographs are insensitive and delay diagnosis.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: suspected metastatic spinal cord compression is an emergency needing urgent whole-spine MRI.
distractorRationale.c: Cancer-related back pain with neurology is not musculoskeletal until compression is excluded.
distractorRationale.d: A month's delay risks permanent paralysis.

questions.explanation: Back pain that worsens lying flat in a patient with a cancer prone to bone metastasis, plus neurological signs, suggests metastatic spinal cord compression. Neurological function is saved only if treatment begins before paralysis.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with ovarian cancer can look after herself and manage light housework but cannot work. She is up and about for most of the day. What is her ECOG performance status?

distractorRationale.a: ECOG 0 means fully active with no restrictions.
distractorRationale.b: ECOG 1 means restricted in strenuous activity but able to do light work.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: ambulatory, self-caring, unable to work and up more than 50 percent of waking hours is ECOG 2.
distractorRationale.d: ECOG 3 means confined to bed or chair more than half of waking hours.

questions.explanation: ECOG 2 describes a patient who is ambulatory and capable of self-care but unable to carry out work activities and who is up and about more than half of waking hours. Performance status influences decisions about chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has a mastectomy for oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer with no evidence of metastases. She is then prescribed endocrine therapy to reduce the risk of the cancer returning. What term describes this treatment?

distractorRationale.a: Neoadjuvant therapy is given before surgery.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: adjuvant therapy follows definitive local treatment to reduce recurrence risk.
distractorRationale.c: Palliative therapy aims to relieve symptoms in incurable disease.
distractorRationale.d: Salvage surgery is surgery after other treatments have failed.

questions.explanation: Adjuvant therapy is given after definitive surgery to target microscopic residual disease and reduce recurrence. Endocrine therapy is one such treatment in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer.

questions.stem: Palliative radiotherapy can be used to relieve pain from bone metastases even when cure is not possible.
questions.explanation: Palliative radiotherapy delivers a short course to a defined field, often relieving bone pain and treating cord compression, without aiming for cure. Goals of treatment, not just the modality, define curative versus palliative intent.

questions.stem: On day 9 after chemotherapy a patient has a temperature of 38.4 C. The full blood count shows a white cell count of 3.2 x 10^9/L with 12 percent neutrophils. Calculate the absolute neutrophil count (answer in 10^9/L).
questions.explanation: ANC = WBC x fraction neutrophils = 3.2 x 0.12 = 0.384 x 10^9/L. This is below 0.5 x 10^9/L, so with fever this is neutropenic sepsis, requiring immediate IV antibiotics. Note that a normal-looking total white cell count can hide severe neutropenia.

questions.stem: A patient is 160 cm tall and weighs 64 kg. Using the Mosteller formula, calculate the body surface area, in m2.
questions.explanation: BSA = sqrt(160 x 64 / 3600) = sqrt(10240 / 3600) = sqrt(2.844) = 1.69 m2. Cytotoxic doses are often prescribed per m2, so BSA links body size to the dose (calculated and verified by oncology pharmacy).

questions.stem: Outline the main modalities of cancer treatment and explain the difference between curative, adjuvant, neoadjuvant and palliative intent.
markingGuide: Modalities: surgery, radiotherapy, cytotoxic chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy
Surgery and radiotherapy are local; chemotherapy, endocrine, targeted and immunotherapy are systemic
Curative: aim to eradicate disease
Adjuvant: after local treatment to reduce recurrence
Neoadjuvant: before local treatment to shrink tumour or treat micrometastases
Palliative: symptom control, quality of life and prolonging survival without cure
Staging (TNM) and tumour biology guide choice
questions.explanation: Choice of modality depends on stage, tumour biology and intent. Naming the goal clarifies how much toxicity is acceptable.

questions.stem: Describe how neutropenic sepsis and metastatic spinal cord compression present and how each is managed in the first hours.
markingGuide: Neutropenic sepsis: fever (38 C or above) or unwell within weeks of chemotherapy, with neutrophils at or below 0.5 x 10^9/L; may lack local signs
Emergency: blood cultures, lactate, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin with tazobactam per NICE unless contraindicated) within 1 hour, fluids, escalate as sepsis
Do not wait for neutrophil count or culture results
MSCC: back pain (thoracic, worse lying or at night, band-like), limb weakness, sensory level, bladder or bowel dysfunction; breast, prostate, lung, myeloma
Urgent whole-spine MRI (NICE within 24 hours if neurological symptoms), corticosteroids per protocol, analgesia, spinal precautions
Urgent oncology or spinal team for radiotherapy or surgery
Neurological function lost before treatment is rarely regained
questions.explanation: Both emergencies are time-critical. Early recognition of symptoms in a patient with cancer is the key to preventing death or permanent disability.

questions.stem: Explain the role of performance status in cancer treatment decisions, giving the ECOG scale and one example of its use.
markingGuide: Performance status is a standardised measure of functional ability that predicts tolerance of treatment and survival

ECOG scale: 0 fully active; 1 restricted strenuous activity; 2 self-care, unable to work, up over 50 percent of day; 3 limited self-care, in bed or chair over 50 percent; 4 completely disabled; 5 dead
ECOG 0 to 1 usually suitable for standard chemotherapy and clinical trials
ECOG 3 to 4 generally derive little benefit from cytotoxic chemotherapy and have high toxicity
Reassess at each cycle; it reflects function not age; a patient whose function improves after symptom control may become eligible
Used with patient preferences and goals in a multidisciplinary decision
questions.explanation: Performance status helps balance benefit against harm. It is dynamic and is combined with the patient's goals when making decisions.
